procedural_history.impugned_order: Two orders of the Additional District Magistrate (Judicial), Saharanpur, dated 6th August, 1963 and 5th October, 1963, dismissing two applications presented by the appellant for dismissing a complaint pending before him for commission of offences under sections 211, 204 and 385 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant, M. L. Sethi, filed a revision application in the High Court at Allahabad desiring the vacation of an order passed by the Sessions Judge of Saharanpur upholding the two orders of the Additional District Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the revision application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: M. L. Sethi appealed to the Supreme Court under a certificate granted by the High Court at Allahabad, seeking to quash the proceedings pending in the Court of the Additional District Magistrate.

issue.issue_text: Whether the bar under Section 195(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code applies to prevent a Magistrate from taking cognizance of a complaint under Section 211 of the Indian Penal Code, when the offence is alleged to have been committed in relation to a proceeding that is merely contemplated and not yet pending or concluded in any court.

law.key_point: The bar on taking cognizance under Section 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. for an offence under Section 211 of the I.P.C. applies only if three specific ingredients exist.
law.evidence: This provision bars taking of cognizance if all the following circumstances exist, viz., (:) that the offence in respect of which the case is brought falls under s. 211 I.P.C.; (2) that there should be a proceeding in any Court; and (3) that the allegation should be that the offence under s. 211 was committed in, or in relation to, such a proceeding. Unless all the three ingredients exist, the bar under s. 195(l)(b) against taking cognizance by the Magistrate... will not come into operation.

law.key_point: The determination of whether the bar applies must be made at the specific point in time when the Magistrate is taking cognizance of the complaint.
law.evidence: Consequently, it is at the stage when a Magistrate is taking cognizance under s. 190 that he must examine the facts of the complaint before him and determine whether his power of taking cognizance under s. 190 has or has not been taken away by cl. (b) of sub-s. (!) of s. 195, Cr. P.C.

law.key_point: The phrase "in relation to" does not extend the bar to proceedings that are merely contemplated or may occur in the future.
law.evidence: There is nothing in the language of the sub-section to indicate that the Legislature also intended lei lay down this bar if a proceeding in a court was still under contemplation... The Magistrate could not be expected to come to a decision whether any such proceeding in any court was under contemplation, and any interpretation of law,. which will make i:s applicability dependent on a future decision to be taken· by some person and thus introduce an element of uncertainty, should be avoided.

application.key_point: The Court analyzed three possible scenarios: (a) no court proceeding exists at all, (b) a proceeding is currently pending, or (c) a proceeding has already concluded.
application.evidence: When examining the question whether there is any proceeding in any Court, there are three situations that can be envisaged. One is that there may be no proceeding in any Court at all. The second is that a proceeding in a Court may actually be pending... The third.is that, though there may be no proceeding pending... there may have beena proceeding which had already concluded...

application.key_point: The Court found that the bar under Section 195(1)(b) applies only to the latter two scenarios (pending or concluded proceedings), but not to the first.
application.evidence: It seems to us that in both the latter two circumstances envisaged above, the bar to taking cognizance under s. 195(l)(b) would· come into operation... In the first circm:µstance envisaged above, when there is no proceeding pending in any Court at all... nor has there been any earlier proceeding which may have been coneluded, the provisions of this sub-section would not be attracted...

application.key_point: Applying this to the issue, if a complaint under Section 211 I.P.C. is filed when the matter is still under police investigation and no judicial order has been made, there is no "proceeding in any Court" at that time.
application.evidence: if a private person, aggrieved by the information given to the police, files a complaint for commission of an offence under s. 211, I. P. C., at any stage before a judicial order has been made by a Magistrate, there can be no question, on the date on which cognizance of that complaint is taken by the Court, of the provisions of s. 195(1) (b) being attracted, because, on that date, there would be no proceeding in any Court in existence...

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the bar under Section 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. does not apply when the offence under Section 211 of the I.P.C. is alleged to have been committed in relation to a proceeding that is merely contemplated and not yet pending or concluded. The Court reasoned that for the bar to be triggered, a 'proceeding in any Court' must either be pending or have already concluded at the time the Magistrate takes cognizance. The mere possibility that a police investigation might later result in a court proceeding is insufficient to attract the bar, as this would introduce an element of uncertainty and is not supported by the language of the statute.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offences under sections 204 and 385, I.P.C., were so inter-mixed with the offence under s. 211, I.P.C., that a trial for those two offences could not proceed if the trial for the offence under s. 211, I.P.C. was barred.

facts: An argument was made before the Supreme Court that the offenses under sections 204 and 385 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) were so inter-mixed with the offense under section 211, I.P.C., that a trial for the first two could not proceed if the trial for the section 211 offense was barred.
application: The Court first considered the primary issue of whether the trial for the offense under section 211, I.P.C., was actually barred by section 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr. P.C.).
The Court came to the decision that cognizance of the offense under section 211, I.P.C., had been rightly taken and that the trial for that offense was not barred or vitiated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that the question of whether the offenses were inter-mixed "need not be dealt with." Since the Court had already decided that the trial for the offense under section 211 was not barred, the condition upon which the issue was based (i.e., that the trial *was* barred) did not exist. Therefore, the Court declined to decide the issue.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the bar under Section 195(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code applies to prevent a Magistrate from taking cognizance of a complaint under Section 211 of the Indian Penal Code, when the offence is alleged to have been committed in relation to a proceeding that is merely contemplated and not yet pending or concluded in any court.
appellant_arguments: The Magistrate is barred from taking cognizance of the complaint under Section 211 IPC due to the provisions of Section 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C.
The bar under Section 195(1)(b) applies even if the offence was committed while the court proceeding was only in contemplation and not yet pending.
The appellant relied on the case of 'In Re Vasudeo Ramchandra Joshi' to argue that the bar is attracted even for offences committed in contemplation of a proceeding.
respondent_arguments: The bar under Section 195 Cr.P.C. is inapplicable because no proceedings were pending in any court when the complaint against the appellant was filed.
The complaint was competent and the Magistrate was within his jurisdiction to take cognizance of it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the offences under sections 204 and 385, I.P.C., were so inter-mixed with the offence under s. 211, I.P.C., that a trial for those two offences could not proceed if the trial for the offence under s. 211, I.P.C. was barred.
appellant_arguments: The offences under sections 204 and 385 IPC are so inter-mixed with the offence under section 211 IPC that a trial for the former two cannot proceed if the trial for the latter is barred by Section 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The text does not specify the respondent's counter-argument on this point, as their primary position was that the main offence under s. 211 was not barred.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The statutory bar preventing a court from taking cognizance of an offense alleged to have been committed in or in relation to a court proceeding applies only if that proceeding is actually pending or has already been taken at the time cognizance is sought. The bar does not extend to situations where a court proceeding is merely under contemplation for the future.
obiter: A statutory limitation on a court's power to take cognizance of an offense is a procedural bar on the court's jurisdiction and does not convert a criminal act into an innocent one.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The bar on taking cognizance of an offence under Section 195(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code applies only when the offence is alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, a proceeding that is either actually pending in a court or has already concluded in a court. The bar does not extend to situations where a court proceeding is merely contemplated but has not yet been instituted, as the applicability of the provision must be determined at the time the Magistrate is asked to take cognizance.
legal_tests_applied: The applicability of the bar under Section 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C. is determined by the status of the related court proceeding at the time the Magistrate takes cognizance of the complaint. The bar operates if, at that moment, a proceeding is either (1) actually pending in any court, or (2) has already concluded in any court. If there is no proceeding in any court at that time, the bar does not apply.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the bar applies to offences committed in relation to a merely contemplated proceeding, stating, 'There is nothing in the language to indicate that the Legislature also intended to lay down this bar if a proceeding in a Court was still under contemplation.'

The appellant's interpretation was deemed impractical and unworkable, as it would 'be laying on the Magistrate a burden which he could not be expected to discharge properly and judicially as no Magistrate could determine in advance of a proceeding in a Court whether the offence... will be an offence which will be found subsequently to have been committed in relation to the contemplated proceeding to be taken thereafter.'

The court found that, as a matter of fact, when the Magistrate took cognizance of the respondent's complaint, 'there was no proceeding in any Court of law, and consequently, at that stage, there could be no question of dignity or prestige of a court of law being upheld or of a private complaint being barred.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court found that a private complaint is permissible if the offence was not committed in relation to an existing or concluded court proceeding. The court stated, 'In the case of cl. (b), there is the clear limitation that private prosecutions are barred only if the offence mentioned in that section was alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any Court. If the offence was not committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any Court, a private complaint is clearly permissible.'

The court affirmed the Magistrate's jurisdiction by focusing on the specific moment of taking cognizance, at which point the factual predicate for the statutory bar (an existing or concluded court proceeding) was absent.
policy_considerations: The court reasoned that the purpose of Section 195, which is to uphold the dignity and prestige of courts, is only engaged once proceedings are actually before a court. The court stated, 'The question of upholding the dignity and prestig~ of courts of law only arises after there are proceedings in the Courts and not at the stage when no such proceedings have been instituted or have come into existence in any Court.'

The court favored an interpretation that promotes legal certainty, stating that accepting the appellant's view on contemplated proceedings 'will introduce an element of uncertainty in the applicability of the law; and such an interpretation must be avoided.'
